description: We are a 5 person Aerospace Engineering and Computering Engineering team skilled in orbital mechanics (MATLAB) and 3D modeling . For the 'Lunar Landing Site Navigator', we are analyzing lunar south pole lighting and communication windows. We are looking for creative Web/App Developers and UI/UX Designers to turn complex NASA data into an interactive interface.
summary:
We have developed an interactive lunar south pole landing-site navigation system focused on three strategic locations relevant to the Artemis era: the Malapert Massif, Faustini Crater, and Shackleton Crater. By integrating topographic data from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with ephemeris calculations from JPL Horizons, the application models 360-degree local horizon profiles—accounting for the absence of atmospheric refraction—and tracks the positions of the Sun and Earth over user-selected dates.

Our tool addresses the inherent complexity of the environment by transforming raw datasets into an intuitive dashboard featuring 2D/3D terrain visualizations and side-by-side scenario comparisons. Users can instantly evaluate solar elevation angles, sunlight duration, time remaining until sunset, and communication windows for direct-to-Earth (DTE) links.

Because the Moon’s axial tilt of approximately 1.54 degrees creates extreme lighting conditions and line-of-sight constraints at the south pole, even minor timing delays or shifts in coordinates can jeopardize power and telemetry. Our solution empowers mission planners and educators to rapidly compare potential landing windows and make agile, data-driven decisions.
details:
Function and Operating Principle

Our application isa decision-support and visualization platform designed to evaluate potential landing sites at the Moon’s south pole, accounting for challenging lighting
conditions and communication constraints. Focusing on three target regions of strategic importance for the Artemis era—the Malapert Massif, Faustini Crater, and Shackleton Crater—the tool allows users to select a specific site (or enter custom coordinates) and define mission dates and durations.

The system integrates high-resolution topography and slope datasets from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with ephemeris (celestial body position) data from NASA JPL Horizons to generate a 360-degree local horizon profile for the chosen location. Since the Moon lacks an atmosphere, our calculations rely on a purely geometric "line-of-sight obstruction" model, which excludes atmospheric refraction. By comparing the azimuth and elevation trajectories of the Sun and Earth against the surrounding terrain, the application calculates solar elevation angles, sunlight duration, the time remaining until sunset or the Earth setting below the horizon, and windows for direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication.

 

Benefits and Intended Impact

While tools such as NASA QuickMap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons provide a wealth of scientific data, conducting rapid scenario comparisons using these platforms often
requires navigating multiple complex interfaces. Our platform bridges this gap
by enabling mission planners, engineers, and researchers to compare alternative
landing dates or backup sites side-by-side in a matter of seconds—a capability
that is critical in scenarios such as launch delays or hardware modifications.
Furthermore, it serves as an accessible educational tool, helping students and
the general public visualize how even minor adjustments to lunar coordinates or
mission timing can significantly impact mission feasibility.

Our team has carefully modeled the physical parameters of the lunar south pole, including the Moon’s ~1.54-degree axial tilt, the absence of atmospheric refraction, terrain slope constraints for safe landing, an illumination threshold of over 50% required for solar-powered operations, and the delicate balance between cryogenic Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs)—which trap water ice at temperatures below 100–110 K—and the nearby illuminated ridges or peaks. The project’s creativity lies in its integration of these multidisciplinary constraints—orbital mechanics, lunar topography, power generation, and DTE (Direct-to-Earth) telemetry—into a single, comparative visual workflow that focuses on the complementary strengths of the Malapert Massif (for communication and illumination), the Faustini Crater (for its high potential for volatiles within Permanently Shadowed Regions, or PSRs), and the Shackleton Crater (for power generation along its rim and access to nearby ice).
